title: The Apostle of Fitness: Jack LaLanne (Legends of the Past)
summary: First episode of the Legends of the Past series: a profile of Jack LaLanne (1914-2011), from a bulimic, sugar-addicted teen to the pioneer of gyms, TV fitness and weights for athletes, who trained until the day before he died at 96. NH draws lessons on whole-food nutrition, training through pain and aging, lifting for life, supersets to failure, and minimal two-meal natural eating that mirrors his own.
claims: LaLanne's creed: exercise is king and nutrition is queen; health is like a bank account where you get out what you put in
As a teen LaLanne was skinny, bulimic and sugar-addicted, often bedridden for up to six months; a Paul Bragg nutrition lecture at 15 turned his life around
If everyone fixed their diet and trained regularly, roughly 90% of health problems would disappear
LaLanne opened one of America's first gyms in 1936 at 21 and was ridiculed by doctors who claimed lifting caused heart attacks and low libido and would make women look like men

Elderly, disabled or amputee people should keep training: an amputee can still build the upper body and the other leg with unilateral work; strength training especially benefits people with cerebral palsy and nervous disorders
Many people take pills to manage symptoms like diabetes, cholesterol, blood pressure or insomnia instead of fixing diet and exercise, which often makes things worse
Processed and junk food can contribute to anxiety and depression, not just physical disease
Exercise, not diet, is the most important pillar for healthy living; he rejects the '80% diet' idea except for certain disorders
Back, elbow and knee pain usually call for training rather than rest; people in their 30s with back pain mostly have weak lower backs and cores
NH says training cures his illnesses and anxiety and strengthens his immune system: when sick, he trains and feels better
LaLanne lifted for over 80 years, from 13 until his death at 96, so lifting two years and claiming you've hit your natural limit is an excuse; train for life
LaLanne trained with supersets only, to failure every session, about two hours a day; NH also uses supersets and failure
Training keeps libido high into old age; LaLanne stayed sexually active into his 80s and 90s
LaLanne was vegetarian apart from fish and eggs, ate two meals a day (e.g. hard-boiled eggs, broth, oatmeal, fruit) and stayed muscular, showing meat is not required for gains
Huge rice-and-chicken meals six times a day came from steroid users; natural dieting is simple; NH himself eats twice a day at about 2,200 kcal
Many vegan or vegetarian fitness influencers are either on drugs, untrained-looking or fat, which hurts the case for those diets
LaLanne's natural physique, with a deep six-pack, strong chest, lats and detailed arms, is attainable by anyone natural; smaller legs suit shorter men
You don't lose muscle at 40; you lose it because you stop training and stop paying attention to diet. LaLanne still had a bicep peak at 60
LaLanne showed muscle and athleticism go together with one-arm handstands and backflips, and pushed resistance training for athletes when it was considered harmful
At 45 LaLanne did 1,000 push-ups and 1,000 chin-ups in 1 hour 22 minutes on TV, finishing despite torn hands
LaLanne swam 2 miles underwater with gear and paddleboarded 30 miles in 10 hours; the boat-pulling feats in his 60s-70s were exaggerated but still impressive
LaLanne pioneered protein powder and the juicer, but you don't need whey to be jacked; he used little; the juicer helps obese people get vitamins easily
LaLanne trained the day before he died of pneumonia at 96, refusing to see a doctor so he could die standing
